title: Cubs, focused on pitching this offseason, show interest in free agent Trevor Rogers: Sources
content:
LAS VEGAS — The Chicago Cubs entered this week’s general managers’ meetings with a clear priority: pitching. As the offseason unfolds, names are starting to emerge.

Chicago has shown early interest in lefty Trevor Rogers, people familiar with the team’s thinking said on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to reveal private discussions. Rogers’ overall numbers from 2026 aren’t anything special. In 169 2/3 innings for the Baltimore Orioles, Rogers posted a 4.03 ERA. His strikeout rate dipped to 22.5 percent, and his groundball rate dropped more than seven points to 38.3 percent. The Cubs would like pitchers who excel in at least one of those areas.

But Rogers seemed to figure things out down the stretch. Over his final 17 starts, he posted a 2.86 ERA with a 26.7 percent strikeout rate. He started using his sweeper more and, in turn, the swing-and-miss jumped. The Cubs surely hope they can get that version of Rogers a bit more consistently.

Chicago is almost starting from scratch with its rotation, and predictably is checking in on nearly every starting pitcher on the market. The Cubs are also busy making smaller signings in minor-league free agency. But heading into 2027, the Cubs need to add multiple arms they feel confident will be no-doubt pieces of their rotation.

Clay Holmes, David Peterson, Matthew Boyd and Shota Imanaga are all free agents. Cade Horton underwent elbow surgery early during the season and isn’t expected back until late in 2027. Justin Steele is healthy but barely pitched the last two years. Ben Brown just underwent a spinal procedure, and Edward Cabrera struggled to stay on the field last summer, and his performance was poor when he did.

“There’s certainly uncertainty,” general manager Carter Hawkins said Tuesday. “We’ve made no secret that we’re going to be looking for pitching this offseason. That’s what the majority of our conversations in the first three hours of the offseason here today have been, and I imagine it’s what a lot of conversations on the trade front will be.”

Right-hander Dustin May has the type of upper-90s stuff Chicago’s rotation has lacked in recent seasons. While he’s logged a solid 278 innings over the last two seasons combined, his upper-4s ERA isn’t as impressive. The Cubs don’t appear to be enamored with May, but with their needs, they won’t rule out anyone at the right price.

The Cubs could revisit talks with right-hander Zac Gallen. The 31-year-old veteran lingered on the market last winter, and the Cubs monitored his free agency into spring training, but ultimately stuck with what they had. Gallen had a poor season (6.07 ERA), saw his strikeout rate plummet to 13.6 percent and battled elbow issues. While he wouldn’t be looked at as a rotation lock, Gallen could compete for a spot in the spring and be considered veteran depth.

Holmes makes a lot of sense for a possible return. His end-of-season command issues (16.1 percent walk rate in his final four starts) were likely an aberration, and his groundball stuff is an obvious plus with the Cubs’ elite infield defense.

“Clay’s got great stuff,” Hawkins said. “He puts the ball on the ground. Outside of the freak injuries that he’s dealt with in the lower half, he’s logged a bunch of innings since he’s moved into a starter’s role. I think he’s a really good fit with our club in terms of the fact that we have such good infield defense, so there’s some nice synergy there. He’s definitely someone we’re interested in.”
